The quiet craft of Japanese carpentry

Japanese temple carpenters, called miyadaiku, build structures that stand for a thousand years without a single nail or screw. Their secret is joinery: interlocking cuts that let timber hold timber, and that let a building flex during earthquakes instead of cracking.

An apprentice spends years sharpening chisels and planes before being trusted with a cut. The tools matter less than the hands, the masters say, but a dull blade ruins hinoki cypress in a single stroke.

Joints that move

The kanawa tsugi joint splices two beams end to end with a wedge that tightens the connection over time. Unlike Western mortise and tenon work, many of these joints are designed to be disassembled, so a damaged beam can be replaced centuries later.

Carpenters cut joints from memory and from drawings passed down within families. Some patterns were kept secret for generations, taught only to the eldest apprentice of each workshop.

Why it lasts

Hinoki cypress grows stronger for two hundred years after it is cut. Combined with joinery that tolerates movement, the wood outlives the people who shaped it. Horyu-ji in Nara, built in the seventh century, is the oldest wooden building in the world.

A building is a tree that has been taught to stand differently.
